# Diabetic kidney disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Renal failure > Diabetic kidney disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/lt0vd3)

---

## Summary

Diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease is a <u>chronic kidney disease</u> (<u>CKD</u>) caused by chronic <u>hyperglycemia</u> and is a major cause of <u>end-stage renal disease</u> (<u>ESRD</u>). In <u>type 1 diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>T1DM</u>), diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease usually occurs 10 years after diagnosis, whereas it can occur at the time of onset of <u>type 2 diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>T2DM</u>). Patients are usually asymptomatic, and diagnosis is based on the presence of <u>albuminuria</u> and/or reduced <u>eGFR</u> and the exclusion of other <u>causes of CKD</u>. Management includes optimization of glycemic control through lifestyle modifications and pharmacotherapy, and <u>management of CKD</u>, including <u>management of hypertension</u> and <u>ASCVD risk factors</u> as needed.

---

## Epidemiology

* Affects up to 40% of adults with <u>diabetes</u> and is a major cause of <u>ESRD</u> [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* Onset varies depending on the type of <u>diabetes</u>: [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* <u>Type 1 DM</u>: Diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease usually occurs approx. 10 years after diagnosis.

* <u>Type 2 DM</u>: may be present at the time of diagnosis




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* <u>Hypertension</u> and blood pressure variability

* Longstanding <u>diabetes</u>

* Inadequate glycemic control

---

## Pathophysiology

Chronic <u>hyperglycemia</u> → glycation (also called <u>non-enzymatic glycosylation</u> or <u>NEG</u>) of the <u>basement membrane</u> (<u>protein glycation</u>) → increased permeability and thickening of the <u>basement membrane</u> and stiffening of the <u>efferent arteriole</u> → hyperfiltration (increase in <u>GFR</u>) → increase in intraglomerular pressure;   → progressive <u>glomerular</u> <u>hypertrophy</u>, increase in renal size, and <u>glomerular</u> scarring (<u>glomerulosclerosis</u>) → worsening of filtration capacity [[3]](/library/cLba98)




![Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system](media/hsoss4c4l60teuv3kzoxrj4o.jpg)

Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

---

## Pathology

Three major histological changes can be seen on <u>light microscopy</u>.  [[4]](/library/II0YVh)[[5]](/library/eZWx0P0)




* Mesangial expansion

* <u>Glomerular basement membrane</u> thickening

* <u>Glomerulosclerosis</u> (later stages)

* Diffuse <u>hyalinization</u> (most common) or

* <u>Pathognomonic</u> nodular glomerulosclerosis (<u>Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules</u>): 

* <u>Glomerular</u> <u>capillary</u> <u>hypertension</u> and hyperfiltration → increase in mesangial matrix → eosinophilic <u>hyaline</u> material in the area of <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillary</u> loops

* Can progressively consume the entire <u>glomerulus</u> → hypofiltration (↓ <u>GFR</u>)





![Diabetic nephropathy](media/soi2g3kjpidl3sd65g2gxtcd.jpg)

Diabetic nephropathy

---

## Clinical features

* Patients are usually asymptomatic in the early stages; some may report foamy urine. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)[[7]](/library/DZW1dP0)

* In the later stages, <u>clinical features of chronic kidney disease</u> (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>, <u>volume overload</u>) may be present. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




* Perform diagnostic studies for patients with positive results from <u>screening for diabetic kidney disease</u>.

* Diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease is confirmed through:

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> showing persistent (≥ 3 months) <u>albuminuria</u> and/or reduced <u>eGFR</u> [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Exclusion of alternative <u>causes of CKD</u> (e.g., <u>hypertensive nephropathy</u>; , <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>); see “<u>Diagnostics for CKD</u>.”

* All patients require <u>CKD staging</u>.

* Refer patients with any of the following to nephrology for further evaluation:  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* <u>Active urinary sediment</u>

* Rapidly progressive <u>albuminuria</u>

* <u>Nephrotic syndrome</u>

* <u>eGFR</u> that is rapidly decreasing or < 30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>

* <u>Indications for renal replacement therapy</u>

* No concurrent <u>diabetic retinopathy</u> in patients with <u>T1DM</u>





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




* <u>Glomerular filtration rate</u> (see also “<u>Diagnostics for CKD</u>”)

* Serum <u>creatinine</u>-based <u>eGFR</u>

* Calculate using the <u>CKD-EPI equation</u>.

* Persistent <u>eGFR</u> < 60 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> is considered abnormal. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Serum <u>cystatin C</u>-based <u>eGFR</u> (alternative); more accurate in <u>transgender</u> patients (see “<u>Principles of transgender health care</u>”) [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Urine studies: spot <u>urine albumin to creatinine ratio</u>  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* Perform in the morning if possible. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* <u>Urine albumin to creatinine ratio</u> â¥ 30 mg/g is considered abnormal.





> [!TIP]
> Repeat <u>laboratory studies</u> after 3–6 months to confirm persistent <u>albuminuria</u> and/or reduced <u>eGFR</u>. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Microalbuminuria</u> may progress to <u>macroalbuminuria</u>. [[8]](/library/-ZWDVP0)

---

## Management

### Approach [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)[[9]](/library/Y_1n5j0)[[10]](/library/Fz1guj0)




* Manage patients as part of a multidisciplinary team.

* Reduce the risk of further progression of <u>CKD</u> with:

* <u>Antihyperglycemic treatment of diabetes</u>

* <u>Lifestyle recommendations for patients with diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Management of hypertension</u>

* Initiate <u>management of CKD</u> and any associated complications (e.g., <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities).

* <u>Screen for additional microvascular complications of diabetes</u> because of the high risk of co-occurrence.

* Arrange scheduled <u>follow-up for diabetic kidney disease</u>.

* Refer to nephrology if patients experience worsening renal function or for assistance managing <u>CKD complications</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease usually occurs together with <u>retinopathy</u> in <u>T1DM</u>. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




> [!TIP]
> Glycemic control and <u>antihypertensive treatment</u> can delay the progression of diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)




### Management of underlying <u>risk factors</u>




#### Modifications to <u>antihyperglycemic treatment</u> in diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)[[10]](/library/Fz1guj0)




* Glycemic targets [[10]](/library/Fz1guj0)

* Measure <u>HbA1c</u> at least twice yearly.  [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* An <u>HbA1c</u> of < 6.5–8% is generally recommended.  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* <u>HbA1c</u> may not be an accurate method of <u>glucose</u> monitoring in patients with an <u>eGFR</u> < 30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>; consider <u>continuous glucose monitoring</u>.

* Pharmacotherapy  [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* <u>T1DM</u>: <u>Insulin</u> dosage may need to be reduced as <u>eGFR</u> declines ; monitor patients for <u>hypoglycemia</u>. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* <u>T2DM</u>

* Choice of treatment depends on <u>eGFR</u>; dosages may need to be adjusted or medications stopped as <u>eGFR</u> declines. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* <u>SGLT-2 inhibitors</u> should be prescribed when possible, as they slow the progression of <u>CKD</u>.  [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* For dosages, see “<u>Noninsulin antidiabetics for T2DM</u>.”





| <br>Treatment of T2DM in patients with CKD [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Recommended pharmacotherapy |
| <u>eGFR</u> ≥ 30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> | <br><br>* First line: <u>metformin</u> AND/OR an <u>SGLT-2 inhibitor</u><br><br>* Consider <u>GLP-1 receptor agonist</u> for patients:<br><br>* Unable to take first-line medications<br><br>* Not reaching glycemic targets on first-line medications<br><br><br> |
| <u>eGFR</u> < 30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> | <br><br>* Discontinue <u>metformin</u>.<br><br>* <u>SGLT2 inhibitors</u> can be continued but should not be initiated in patients with <u>eGFR</u> < 20 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>.<br><br>* Selected <u>dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors</u>, <u>GLP-1 receptor agonists</u>, <u>insulin</u>, <u>thiazolidinediones</u>, and short-acting <u>sulfonylureas</u> can be used.<br><br><br> |
| Patients with a <u>kidney transplant</u> | <br><br>* Paucity of evidence to guide practice<br><br>* Follow guidelines for treatment according to <u>eGFR</u>.<br><br>* <u>SGLT2 inhibitors</u> may theoretically increase the risk of severe infection in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>SGLT-2 inhibitors</u> improve renal and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with <u>T2DM</u> and <u>CKD</u> or <u>albuminuria</u>; their use is even recommended for patients who meet <u>HbA1c</u> targets. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




> [!WARNING]
> Adjust the dosing of <u>antihyperglycemic medications</u> in patients with reduced <u>eGFR</u> as needed. <u>Metformin</u> is contraindicated in patients with an <u>eGFR</u> < 30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




#### <u>Management of ASCVD</u> <u>risk factors</u> for patients with diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




Patients should undergo <u>management of ASCVD risk factors in CKD</u> with the following modifications for <u>hypertension management</u>:  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




* Patients with <u>albuminuria</u>: for dosages see “<u>Antihypertensive therapy</u>.”

* First-line: <u>RAS inhibitors</u> (<u>ACE inhibitors</u> or <u>angiotensin receptor blockers</u>)

* Titrate up gradually to the maximum tolerated dose. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Monitor serum <u>potassium</u> and <u>creatinine</u>; do not discontinue until <u>creatinine</u> levels increase by > 30% from baseline.[[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[11]](/library/qTdC760)

* Combination <u>antihypertensive therapy</u>: Consider if blood pressure is not controlled with an <u>RAS inhibitor</u>. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* <u>Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists</u> PLUS <u>RAS inhibitor</u>: for patients with persistent <u>albuminuria</u> refractory to therapy  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[11]](/library/qTdC760)

* Patients without <u>albuminuria</u>: : Initiate <u>first-line antihypertensive medication</u> (i.e., <u>RAS inhibitors</u>, <u>thiazide diuretics</u>, or <u>calcium channel blockers</u>). [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not prescribe <u>RAS inhibitors</u> to <u>normotensive</u> patients, unless they have <u>albuminuria</u>, as trials have not shown a renoprotective effect in this cohort. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[11]](/library/qTdC760)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists</u> are associated with improved cardiovascular and renal outcomes. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>ACE inhibitors</u> and <u>angiotensin receptor blockers</u> are potential <u>teratogens</u> and should not be used in pregnant patients. Avoid use in women of childbearing age who do not use <u>contraception</u>. [[12]](/library/ajdQ_p0)




### <u>Management of CKD</u> in patients with <u>diabetes</u> [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)[[10]](/library/Fz1guj0)




* Educate patients on diabetic <u>kidney</u> disease. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Advise patients that some treatments may cause an initial decline in <u>eGFR</u>.

* Encourage patients to attend all recommended follow-up appointments.

* See also “<u>Managing chronic conditions</u>.”

* Provide nutritional advice; consider dietitian consultation. [[11]](/library/qTdC760)

* Adjust protein intake based on <u>CKD stage</u>.  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[11]](/library/qTdC760)

* Consider <u>sodium</u> restriction (below 2–2.3 g/day)  and <u>potassium</u> restriction , if necessary. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)[[11]](/library/qTdC760)

* Adjust the dosage of <u>renally cleared medications</u> based on <u>eGFR</u> and avoid <u>nephrotoxins</u>.

* Ensure patients are up-to-date on <u>vaccinations</u> (see “<u>Immunization schedule</u>”).  [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)





### Follow-up for diabetic kidney disease




* Reassess <u>ASCVD risk factors</u> every 3–6 months. [[6]](/library/-G1Dbi0)

* Patients with <u>eGFR</u> ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* Mild to moderate <u>albuminuria</u>: Monitor annually (see “<u>Screening for diabetic kidney disease</u>”).

* Severe <u>albuminuria</u>: Perform <u>screening for diabetic kidney disease</u> three times a year.

* Patients with <u>eGFR</u> < 60 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>: Regularly assess for <u>complications of CKD</u>. [[2]](/library/6bdjuo0)

* Check BP and assess for <u>signs of fluid overload</u> at each visit.

* Check <u>eGFR</u>, urinary <u>albumin</u>, serum <u>electrolytes</u>, <u>CBC</u>, and markers for <u>metabolic bone disease</u>: 

* Every 6–12 months in <u>stage 3 CKD</u>

* Every 3–5 months for <u>stage 4 CKD</u>

* Every 1–3 months in <u>stage 5 CKD</u>
